beats.vo_text: Somewhere in the waters off the north coast of Scotland, there's a patch of sea with nothing on it. No dive boats. No buoys marking a popular wreck site.
beats.visual_intent: Cinematic drone shot over a desolate, cold, dark grey Scottish coastal sea under an overcast sky.

beats.vo_text: Just one lonely marker, and a warning painted on it that most people never get close enough to read.
beats.visual_intent: Close-up shot of a single green navigational buoy bobbing in choppy dark water, with warning text stenciled on its side.

beats.vo_text: Beneath that buoy, in water shallow enough that recreational divers could reach it in minutes, lies one of the best-preserved battleships in the world. Over eight hundred men are still inside it.
beats.visual_intent: Underwater medium shot looking up past a green mooring chain into deep, murky green water.

beats.vo_text: And for more than forty years, it has been illegal — under UK law — for almost anyone to go down and see it.
beats.visual_intent: Dramatic underwater spotlight beam cutting through murky dark water, illuminating a rusted steel hull.

beats.vo_text: Every single day, somewhere beneath that ship, a small amount of oil still rises to the surface. It's been doing that for over eighty years.
beats.visual_intent: Macro shot of iridescent oil droplets slowly detaching and rising upward toward the light.

beats.vo_text: Nobody has fully explained how long it will keep happening — or what happens when it stops.
beats.visual_intent: Surface water shot showing a faint, shimmering oily sheen spreading across dark, cold waves.

beats.vo_text: To understand why this wreck is off-limits, you have to go back to October 1939 — five weeks into the Second World War — to a body of water called Scapa Flow.
beats.visual_intent: Archival sepia-toned photograph of a wartime naval harbor under cloudy skies.

beats.vo_text: Scapa Flow is a natural harbor in the Orkney Islands, ringed by land on almost every side. For decades it had been the Royal Navy's main fleet anchorage in the north.
beats.visual_intent: Wide aerial shot of a calm, enclosed Scottish sea loch surrounded by rolling green hills.

beats.vo_text: The entrances were narrow, the currents were vicious, and the Navy believed that made the anchorage effectively unreachable by enemy submarines. They were wrong.
beats.visual_intent: Dramatic close-up of a vintage Royal Navy compass spinning and shuddering against a dark background.

beats.vo_text: On the night of October 13th, a German submarine — U-47, commanded by 30-year-old Günther Prien — threaded its way through one of those impossible gaps.
beats.visual_intent: Archival black-and-white photo of a German U-boat cutting through dark, choppy ocean waters at night.

beats.vo_text: Inside Scapa Flow, at anchor, sat HMS Royal Oak — a Revenge-class battleship built back in 1914, carrying over a thousand men.
beats.visual_intent: Historical blueprint and photograph collage of a massive dreadnought battleship at anchor.

beats.vo_text: In the early hours of October 14th, Prien fired his first spread of torpedoes. Most of the crew barely noticed — the explosion was small, and far from the magazines.
beats.visual_intent: Low-key cinematic reenactment lighting of a submarine periscope view looking toward a distant anchored warship silhouette.

beats.vo_text: Prien turned his boat around, reloaded, and fired again. This time there was no ambiguity. A second salvo struck the ship's side directly.
beats.visual_intent: Dramatic graphic representation of torpedo tracks converging on a battleship hull silhouette in dark blue water.

beats.vo_text: Royal Oak began to capsize almost immediately — she rolled and went under in a matter of minutes, far too fast for most of the crew to escape.
beats.visual_intent: Cinematic underwater motion graphic showing a massive battleship hull rolling over and sinking into the abyss.

beats.vo_text: Eight hundred and thirty-three men and boys died that night. Some were as young as fourteen. It remains one of the deadliest single losses in Royal Navy history.
beats.visual_intent: Solemn memorial visual with stacked typographic counters and archival sailor portraits fading into shadow.

beats.vo_text: A nearby drifter, the Daisy II, managed to pull nearly 400 men from the freezing water. But for the majority of the crew, there was no time.
beats.visual_intent: Archival black-and-white photograph of exhausted sailors wrapped in blankets on a rescue vessel deck.

beats.vo_text: Royal Oak came to rest upside down in just over 30 meters of water — shallow enough that, in theory, any certified recreational diver could reach her.
beats.visual_intent: 3D bathymetric cross-section graphic showing a sunken ship resting upside down on the seabed 30 meters below the surface.
